collection.description: A fever is going around the village.

ask.text:
A fever is going around the village. Not a dangerous one, mostly, but everyone has it at once, and everyone needs (subject), the healer, at once.
(subject) has not eaten a hot meal in four days. (subject.He/She) has not slept a full night in four days. (subject.He/She) walks from hut to hut with (subject.his/her) bag of herbs, from dawn until long after dark, and then gets woken up twice in the night.
This morning, while grinding herbs at (subject.his/her) table, (subject) fell asleep. Standing up. With the grinding stone still in (subject.his/her) hand. (subject.He/She) only woke when (subject.he/she) dropped it on (subject.his/her) foot. How can the village help (subject) before (subject.he/she) collapses?

choices.label: Ask the Healer What Is Draining Them
Bring a Builder to the Sick Hut

text_only.reason: the word in the owner's story; what changes in the game is the ending's own EFFECT line (the ledger), so this word alone changes nothing

c1o1.text: Between spoonfuls, (subject) realizes that half the exhaustion isn't the healing at all. It's the walking: back and forth between sick huts scattered across the whole village, carrying everything. If the sickbeds were together under one roof, (subject.he/she) could see everyone at once. (subject) helps lash up a simple shelter for the sick that afternoon, learning a practical building lesson along the way, and that night, (subject.he/she) sleeps for six hours.

c1o2.text: (subject) explains that nobody told (subject.him/her) the herb gatherers were sick too. So (subject.he/she) has been gathering herbs at dawn, and healing all day, and grinding herbs all night. It was a missed message, not anyone shirking. Within an hour, two healthy villagers have volunteered to gather herbs until the gatherers recover.

c1.text: Someone sits (subject) down, puts a bowl of hot stew in (subject.his/her) hands, and won't let (subject.him/her) get up until (subject.he/she) has eaten it and answered one question: what's the worst part?...

c2o1.text: The trainees take the night calls, nervous but careful, and come to (subject) only for the truly worrying cases. The work carries on at a pace (subject) can survive. By the end of the week, the fever has passed, the trainees are much more confident, and (subject) has had three hot meals.

c2o2.text: On the first night, the trainees mix up two patients, giving one the other's tea. Nobody is harmed: both teas were for fever, one just tasted worse. But everyone agrees to fix the arrangement in the morning, with a clear list of who gets what, written on a board by the door.

c2.text: The village asks (subject)'s trainee healers to take over the night calls, so (subject) can sleep...

c3o1.text: (builder) teaches (subject) how to lash a raised sickbed: a wooden frame at waist height, with a woven top, so the healer doesn't have to kneel and bend over every patient. They build four together. (subject)'s back stops aching for the first time in years, and (subject.he/she) learns a lot about building in the process, enough to build more on (subject.his/her) own.

c3o2.text: (builder) admits, somewhat sheepishly, that (subject.he/she) fainted the one time (subject.he/she) tried to help a healer, at the sight of a cut. "Went down like a felled tree." It shouldn't make (subject) feel better, but somehow it does, and (subject.he/she) laughs for the first time all week.

c3.text: (builder) watches (subject) bending over a patient on a low floor mat, wincing, and has an idea...
